paper_title: PReMind: When Personal Memory Meets Visual Hazards

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Personalized vision-language assistants use visual observations and personal memories to provide advice tailored to the user. When the observed scene contains a physical hazard, personal context, such as allergies, medical conditions, or mobility constraints, can change what help is appropriate. Responding appropriately therefore requires recognizing the visible hazard and applying the relevant person's information. We introduce PReMind-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates this combination across diverse hazards and personal-memory conditions. It separately measures memory access, grounding, abstention, and hazard response, and assesses joint success on interdependency cases. Existing models often satisfy one requirement while failing the other, and training only for safety or personalization leaves a gap in joint success. We therefore propose PReMind, a two-phase reinforcement learning framework that combines on-demand and forced-call interactions (memory always retrieved) to jointly train grounded memory use and hazard response. At 4B, PReMind raises joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base on the interdependency set and improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention on the main test. Joint-success gains persist under forced-call evaluation and under a second LLM judge across three Phase II seeds; averaged over these seeds, joint success also improves on unseen hazard groups. These findings highlight the need to evaluate and train personal assistants to connect visual evidence with the relevant person's context.

Content warning: this paper shows synthetic images of hazards, such as fire and injuries, that some readers may find distressing. 1. Introduction Visionlanguage assistants use personal context to recognize familiar people, pets and belongings across scenes [1, *Corresponding author. The name PReMind reflects the goal of alerting the user to risk before it develops into larger emergency. 8, 23]. Recent methods use reinforcement learning (RL) and accumulated imagetext context [25, 27]. These assistants may also encounter urgent situations, such as an injured family member seen on home camera or household hazard in users photo. Personal memory can inform what help is appropriate in these situations. An image may show that someone has fallen, while memory records health condition, mobility constraint, or support arrangement that the image cannot reveal. The assistant must recognize the hazard, identify the person, and use the relevant personal fact  (Fig. 1)  . Despite rapid progress in visual personalization and safety, prior benchmarks have rarely evaluated these dimensions together. Personalization benchmarks assess whether answers reflect user facts, but rarely assess situational safety. Conversely, safety benchmarks evaluate visual risk detection or over-refusal [15, 28, 36, 42], while personalized-safety frameworks rely on text-only profiles or static hidden context [33, 40]. None of the prior evaluations in Table 1 jointly scores whether model identifies the person, retrieves their fact, and uses it in responding to the hazard. Evaluating this setting requires deciding when to access memory, matching visible people, pets, and belongings to their own memories, and handling hazards while avoiding false alarms on safe requests. We distinguish two kinds of safety: [ Definitions: two kinds of safety Personalization safety means using personal memory appropriately: consulting it when needed but not introducing irrelevant personal facts into answers that require no memory (adaptive retrieval), using the correct persons or objects facts (grounding), and asking or abstaining when the evidence is missing (abstention). Situational safety means responding appropriately to visible hazards while avoiding unwarranted warnings or safety escalation on safe requests. Figure 1. Scene and personal-memory examples. Each row shows query image, user request, retrieved personal memory, and response snippets from PReMind-4B and comparison models. Personalization-focused and Safety-focused describe each comparator answers behavior, not trained specialists. Memory tags indicate memory type (Table S.4). Interdependency refers to cases whose references combine visible hazard with personal fact. Memory may inform precautions, assistance, or information passed to responders. We introduce PReMind-Bench to measure each requirement independently and assess whether an answer satisfies both under its reference criteria. By decoupling memory access and grounding failures from hazard-response errors, PReMind-Bench provides fine-grained diagnosis of assistant behavior. We develop PReMind through two-phase RL framework that mixes on-demand and forced-call interactions in both phases, first learning memory access, grounded fact use, and hazard response, then learning situational adaptation that links the retrieved memory to what the image shows. Our main contributions are: Problem and benchmark. We introduce PReMindBench, diagnostic benchmark to evaluate how personal visionlanguage assistants combine visible hazard handling with relevant personal memory. PReMindBench uses paired comparisons and scores memory access, grounding, abstention, hazard response, and joint success separately. The benchmark covers safe requests, visible acute hazards, non-acute risks, and risks revealed by personal memory, with interdependency cases whose references require hazard response and person-specific 2 Table 1. Comparison with prior work. Among the compared works, only PReMind-Bench evaluates personalization safety and situational safety together, including interdependency cases and the memory-access decision.

Results are reported by hazard group, request type, and interdependency case rather than as one pooled score. Analysis. Existing models often meet one requirement but not the other: safety-only models overlook personal facts, while personalization-only models miss visible hazards. Scoring memory access, grounding and hazard response separately shows where each model fails, and these failures motivate joint training. Method and model. We propose PReMind, two-phase RL framework that jointly trains memory access and hazard response under both on-demand and forced-call interactions. Under GPT-6-Luna evaluation, PReMind raises joint success over its base by about 15 points at 4B (mean over three Phase II seeds). Gains persist under forced-call evaluation. 2. Related Work Personalization. Visual personalization first learned concepts from few images through embeddings or learned tokens [1, 23], then retrieved them from an imagetext database [8]. Recent methods train with RL using verifiable rewards instead of imitating reference answers, as in RePIC for personalized captioning [25] and CoViP for interpreting new images through the users accumulated imagetext context [27]. Memory agents store and retrieve user context across long interactions [6, 18, 19, 24, 39]; M2A and M3-Agent decide when to query memory, and M3-Agent learns this decision with RL [6, 19]. Omni-Persona tests queries about absent personas [26]. Adaptive retrieval decides whether to retrieve from text query [2, 10, 20], not from an image. These works do not jointly score memory3 access decisions and hazard responses  (Table 1)  . PReMindBench scores both, and PReMind uses RL [32, 41] to couple grounded memory use with hazard response (Sec. 5). Safety. Multimodal safety benchmarks evaluate visually grounded risk, unsafe responses and over-refusal [15, 28, 36, 42]. Personalized-safety research further shows that safe advice depends on the users circumstances [40], while PACE tests retrieval of personal constraints from textual knowledge base [13]. MPS-Bench extends personalized safety to images, including cases where hidden user profile makes an apparently benign request risky [33]. These works do not jointly evaluate identifying the person in view, retrieving that persons memory and using it in an acutehazard response. Our interdependency cases evaluate this combination: the image supplies hazard evidence and memory supplies person-specific context for the response. 3. Each request has annotated access c(x): call if its reference uses personal fact, direct if the image suffices, or any if memory may inform but does not decide the answer. PReMind-Bench Each scene pairs visual environment with personal memory store and multiple related requests. Memory need, target evidence availability, and physical risk vary independently  (Fig. 2)  , without explicit cues to the assistant. 4.1. Scenes, memories, and requests Scenes and memories. We composite individuals, pets and belongings into frames captured for 3D reconstruction in Mip-NeRF 360 and Zip-NeRF [3, 4] (ten environments; 120 training/test viewpoints). Figure S.2 shows training/validation and test scenes. Scene geometry guides the edits. Memory stores contain targets, same-type lookalikes and distractor concepts. Look-alikes match finegrained attributes (e.g., age group and gender) but carry different facts about the same requested action, so the assistant must identify the person rather than match the topic. Figure 2. Scenario map. Every request includes an image. (a) single visual scene and its memory store support requests requiring different evidence. (b) Requests are categorized by required evidence: personal fact (PF), safety knowledge (SK), both, or scene only (SO). CALL requests require memory retrieval, whereas DIRECT requests do not. Risk (safe vs. unsafe) varies independently. Requests. Requests are user questions or instructions about the scene. They omit names, decisive personal facts, and explicit hazard cues. Deciding whether to offer someone snack may require memory; counting visible plates does not. Some requests test whether the assistant uses the current image instead of remembered habit to answer. Safe requests. Safe requests carry no risk indicated by the scene or relevant personal memory. Labeling them unsafe (ˆr = unsafe) counts as false alarm; memory-access and abstention requirements still apply. Unsafe requests. Acute hazards span five groups: person down, heat/electrical/chemical, mechanical, animals and environment. Non-acute visual risks (e.g., trip hazards) require actionable precautionary advice. Other risks (e.g., allergies or medical contraindications) are revealed only by personal memory. We evaluate acute-hazard responses for adequacy and critical harm using public safety guidance (App. S.1.2). Interdependency cases. Interdependency cases pair visible hazard with person-specific fact used in the reference (e.g., medical conditions, assistance needs, or rescue equipment locations; Fig. 1). References cover tailored advice and information passed to responders. Hazardresponse references specify expected actions and acceptable alternatives without requiring verbatim answers. Lookalike entries carry topic-aligned distractor facts to evaluate misattribution. Control cases pairing non-hazardous images with identical memory entries test for false-positive safety escalations. Verification. Automated review checks identity, visual evidence, memory dependence, information leakage and risk. Unresolved examples are and model-assisted 4 Figure 3. Benchmark statistics. (a) Hazard groups in training/validation versus test; H2H5 appear only at test time, and all training acute scenes, including Phase II thermal-illness cases, show collapsed or distressed people (H1). (b) Distribution of acute hazard groups in the test set. (c) Breakdown of decisive personal memory types across interdependency cases (Table S.4). removed; every test example, including its image, memory and reference answer, is manually verified. Visual-input ablations show that both image sources matter: removing reference images sharply lowers grounding and joint success while largely retaining hazard adequacy, and gray query images drop joint success to near zero (Table S.19). 4.2. Contrasts, splits, and scale To test memory need, paired requests share scene and memory store but ask different questions. To create targetabsent cases, paired examples share the scene and request but remove the target memory. These pairs help distinguish memory use from responses based only on the image and user request. No test target person serves as training target, though objects and pets may recur. Training includes person-down hazards so that the model learns how to respond to an unsafe scene; the other hazard groups appear only at test time to measure transfer  (Fig. 3)  . The main test has 1,024 requests (384 acute); 999 are scored after retrieval-based exclusions, and six retrieval misses are relabeled target-absent. With interdependency cases and hazard-free controls, the test set has about 1.1k cases. Interdependency evaluation overlaps with main-test cases but avoids double-counting in statistics. App. S.1 gives construction, verification and release details. 4.3. Evaluation metrics Memory access and citations are scored by rules; LLM judges assess hazard response and memory-informed effect using fixed rubrics, annotated scene descriptions, and reference actions. Rates use the applicable population, excluding missing judge outputs (App. S.2.2). Memory use. Call Balanced Accuracy (Call BA) averages recall on memory-required and image-only requests; always or never calling scores 50%. On target-present requests, Citation Set F1 (Cite F1) compares cited indices ˆS with target indices S; missed call scores zero. Fact Use (sfact) credits stated target fact with its entry cited. Misattribution (smis) flags use of look-alikes fact. On target-absent requests, Abstention (sabs) requires clarification or abstention that states uncertainty or asks question, without citations, asserted names or look-alike facts. On acute requests, safety escalation also qualifies. Hazard response and joint success. For acute requests, judge assigns h: adequate, generic-only, none or contraindicated. Adequacy (sadq) indicates an adequate response; Critical Harm (scrit) flags an instruction likely to cause death or serious injury or to obstruct lifesaving care. Both are needed: giving no useful advice can avoid harm while failing adequacy. Memory-Informed Effect (MIE; smie) credits the target fact in advice or handoff, without call or citation check. Each is per-example indicator; its mean is the corresponding rate. On interdependency cases, Joint Success Rate (JSR) averages: sjoint = sadq (1 scrit) smie (1 smis). (2) response may fail joint success by omitting the personal fact when its hazard response is adequate and noncritical. False alarms on safe requests and hazard responses on hazard-free twins are reported separately (App. S.6 and Table S.18). Confidence intervals (95%) resample query images with all their requests, accounting for intra-image 5 correlation. 5. PReMind: Jointly Learning Memory Use and Hazard Response We train memory access, grounding, and hazard response to improve joint success. PReMind uses group-relative DAPO-style RL [41] in two phases: Phase learns these capabilities jointly, and Phase II targets situational adaptation on harder memory-dependent cases. Neither JSR nor MIE is directly rewarded; MIE guides replay selection. Interaction regimes. For each request, we sample group of episodes from two regimes: on-demand episodes sample the access decision to update both factors of Eq. (1), whereas forced-call episodes fix = call and mask firstturn decision tokens, training evidence use even when the policy would skip retrieval. Inference is on demand. Reward design. An assistant may address the hazard using the wrong persons fact, or recall the fact while ignoring the hazard. Each requirement also has cheap shortcuts, such as always calling memory, always abstaining or giving one stock instruction for every scene. (4) Grounding and abstention. Rgnd uses the rule-based checks of Sec. 4.3. It credits citing and stating target facts when the target is present (S = ) and abstaining (sabs) when required target is missing (S = ); it penalizes misattribution (smis), ungrounded personal claims, and needless abstention. Hazard response. RL includes both safe and unsafe requests. The policy never sees reference answers during training. An LLM judge scores sampled responses against the reference actions of training requests. On acute hazards, Rhaz ranks scene-specific actions above generic advice and generic advice above ignoring the hazard, and penalizes contraindicated instructions. For safe requests, labeling the request as unsafe or issuing unsupported hazard warnings is penalized to discourage indiscriminate safety responses. 6 Two-phase training. Phase optimizes Eq. (3) with penalty for unconditioned recovery-position or roll instructions. The resulting policy falls back on stock phrases: of the 337 acute answers whose scene does not call for staying still, 20.5% advise it, vs. 1.8% for the base (rule-based count; Table S.8). It also has higher critical-harm rate than after Phase II (12.2% vs. 8.7%; Table 4). Phase II resets the optimizer and adds fact bonus for stating and citing the decisive fact (sfact = 1), and three refinements: (i) Curriculum filtering. We set each cases difficulty from group of eight answers sampled from the Phase model. Cases it always solves are dropped, partly solved cases enter from easy to hard, and cases it never solves come last. (ii) Experience replay. Phase II reintroduces hard cases where the model failed to use relevant memory facts (smie = 0), using judge labels for sampling, not as reward. Groups containing both full-fact and omission answers are replayed once. (iii) Action-prioritized hazard credit. Hazard-first credit goes only to an opening that names an action specific to the scene, and stock phrases used regardless of the scene, such as telling everyone to stay still or only to call for help, are penalized. Training details are in App. S.3. 6. Experiments We compare PReMind-4B with open-source VLMs, personalized models (CoViP-8B and RePIC-7B), and closedsource models (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1-Sol, and GPT-6Luna). Luna judges hazard responses during training and evaluation at medium reasoning effort; Sonnet 5.5 rejudges interdependency responses as second judge. Unless stated otherwise, we report seed 0 with on-demand top-four retrieval and greedy decoding. We focus on 4B, for which we conduct the full set of controlled evaluations; PReMind-9B results and Phase II seed variation are reported in App. S.4. Human volunteers judge that personal facts change the appropriate action in 52 of 56 cases, supporting reference relevance without clinical validation (App. S.5). 7. Conclusion and Limitations Conclusion. PReMind-Bench highlights gap in personal assistants when responses require both visual hazard recognition and personal memory. By separating memory access, person-specific grounding, abstention, and hazard response, the benchmark exposes failures hidden by single-axis evaluation. Joint training with on-demand and forced-call interactions raises joint success from 12.9% for the 4B base to 28.6% for PReMind-4B; gains persist under forced-call 8 evaluation and under second LLM judge. These findings support further research on personalized assistants that jointly account for visual hazards and individual needs. Future work includes broader environments, continual memory adaptation, and egocentric video. Limitations. Despite multi-view coverage, the benchmark uses ten edited environments (four in test) with fictitious memories, and reference actions lack independent clinical validation. Primary LLM judges evaluate against annotated scene descriptions and reference rubrics rather than raw images. PReMind more often labels safe requests as unsafe and makes more unnecessary memory calls than its Interdependency harm reduction is not established, base. and harm comparisons depend on the judge. Stored facts are assumed truthful; outdated, conflicting or adversarial memories and provenance checks remain for future study.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: We used GPT-6-Sol to draft benchmark requests, fictitious personal memories and reference answers, and gpt-image-2 to edit scene images (Sec. 4.1). GPT-6Luna and Claude Sonnet 5.5 judge responses for evaluation, and GPT-6-Luna also scores rewards in training (Secs. 4.3 and 5). Closed-source LLMs are also evaluated as reference systems; App. S.8 lists every model and its role. LLMbased coding assistants (Claude Code and Codex) helped write experiment code and edit the manuscript text for clarity and length. For related work, LLMs assisted with paper search and summarization; the authors chose and verified every cited paper and the claims attributed to it. No LLM was used for research ideation. Hazard types H2H5 are reserved for test evaluation (Fig. 3a). Training acute scenes exclusively depict collapsed or distressed individuals, including Phase II thermal illness cases (App. S.3.2). Environmental acute hazards in H2 (fire, electrical, chemical) are entirely unseen during training, matching the experimental splits in Tables 3 and S.17. Taxonomy of personal memory. Ground-truth facts in interdependency cases fall into five primary categories: Health & Medication (medical conditions/treatments), Belongings & Know-how (location of rescue items or utility shut-offs), Physical Limitation (mobility constraints), Behavior Habit (recurring tendencies), and Past Experience (historical incidents). Memory stores also contain preferences and emergency contacts (Table S.4). Health facts specifying rescue equipment locations are categorized under Belongings & Know-how when expected actions involve item deployment, and under Health otherwise. Interdependency design principles. Each interdependency case pairs visible hazard with target memory fact. Construction prioritized five criteria: 1. Latent context: Physical threats are visually observable, whereas personal facts remain unobservable in the image frame. 2. Person specificity: Personal facts describe the target rather than general reactions common to most people. 3. Actionable relevance: Authoring prioritized facts expected to inform advice, precautions or responder handoffs. This criterion does not independently establish that generic safe advice is insufficient. 4. Entity grounding: Stored facts belong to the visual entity (or their direct belongings/pets) visually detected in the scene. 5. Topic-matched look-alikes: In 95 of 100 test-only variants, the online top-four context includes same-topic entries about other people, matched in length and risk. The other five contain no other person in the top four. Topic, length and negation rules perform near chance on these look-alikes. Illustrative authoring targets include: Seizure management: Integrates seizure history and emergency medication locations into immediate scene safety guidance. Chemical fumes: Combines chemical exposure avoidance with rescue inhaler locations, subject to safe scene access. Cardiac collapse: Pairs responsiveness/breathing checks with home AED locations. The final evaluation set includes main-test cases and testonly variants. Control cases (n = 12) pair non-hazardous visual scenes with identical memory stores and requests to verify that agents do not trigger false-positive safety escalations. Verification included automated shortcut checks, review of fact relevance, look-alike balancing and separate model-assisted reference checks. These text-based reviews preceded final scoring and did not independently validate clinical correctness or action necessity. Flawed samples were corrected or removed. S.1.6. Masked edits use gpt-image-2, with target placement guided by scene geometry or size reference. Construction text stages use GPT-6-Sol to draft requests and reference answers from the image and matching memory entry; the checks below and author verification determine which items are retained. Deterministic checks test label consistency, fact support and citations, and the image-aware review does not see the authors rationale. Failed components are repaired and reviewed again. Items that remain unresolved are removed. Calm and panic-style requests are assigned independently of labels. Construction summaries are in App. S.9, and source rights and release terms in App. S.7. Requests are framed in either explicit or implicit forms: explicit requests specify target action, whereas implicit requests leave task specification to scene interpretation. Neither style reveals entity identities, decisive personal facts, or visual hazard cues. Results are not reported separately by style. Image-only requests. Active scene-only (SO) items comprise visual queries whose answers depend strictly on observable spatial locations or environmental states that personal memory cannot alter. Queries whose answers could legitimately incorporate personal contextsuch as neutral requests or general hazard adviceare classified as neutral. Habit-over-image distractors. To evaluate memory vision trade-offs, many active SO items are paired with distractor facts representing habitual user behaviors (e.g., an objects routine location or an individuals usual posture). Distractor facts are assigned to same-category look-alike memory entries that are never cited in ground-truth references. Requests adopt situational phrasing that naturally evokes the stored habit (e.g., Im heading out and need the tote bagwhere is it right now?), requiring the model to prioritize real-time visual observations over remembered routines. Distractor exposure is tracked independently across memory conditions, and priming diagnostics are restricted to scenarios where distractor entries are actively present in context (App. S.4). Verification and label consistency. Beyond automated model-assisted review, we manually verified the query image, memory store, and reference answer for every test example. Active SO items are restricted to unambiguously observable objects; items are retained only if ground-truth answers are visually confirmed and consistent with reference annotations across related scene queries. Unresolved items are reclassified as neutral. All benchmark items passed automated validation scripts verifying action taxonomy labels, citation indices, and target-absent annotations against ground-truth reference sets. S.2. Evaluation Protocol, Metrics, and Judges This section details the scores in Sec. 4.3, their populations and judge checks. Figure S.6. Two-turn memory interaction. The agent decides whether to call memory from the image and request, then answers with any retrieved context. Visible acute hazards require response even when personal evidence is missing; memory call alone does not warn the user. but the request still requires memory call; the agent must handle the missing personal information without guessing. For broad environmental queries, personal context may offer helpful background without governing response correctness. These neutral queries accept either decision, are excluded from retrieval accuracy metrics, and are evaluated on their answers (App. S.2.2). S.2.1. Interaction Protocol and Evidence S.2.2. Metrics and Scoring Populations Sec. 3 defines the retrieval access action c, the predicted response tuple = (ˆr, ˆa, ˆz, ˆS), the annotated access label c(x), and target citation indices S; Sec. 4.3 details downstream metric implementations. Forced-call evaluation control. Rows on which the model called memory retain their first-turn text. Otherwise, the first turn is fixed to the call tag. The retrieved entries are unchanged. Memory necessity and evidence conditions. The agent should call memory when the request and referencesupported content need personal memory, and should answer without memory for active scene-only requests. If retrieval misses the target, no entry counts as gold support, Personalization and memory use. Each response is tagged with one action type: direct answer, clarification, abstention or safety escalation. Call BA is the mean of needed-call recall and no-call accuracy on active imageonly requests. Citation Set F1 (Cite F1) measures set overlap between predicted indices ˆS and target indices [27]; Fact Use (sfact) requires simultaneous target assertion and citation. Citation normalization also accepts forms such as Memory 4. Both metrics evaluate end-to-end performance and assign zero score following unattempted required calls. Misattribution (smis) flags incorrect assertion of look-alike facts present in context, accounting for speculative hedging. Abstention (sabs) measures correct handling of missing evidence [29]: clarify or abstain with uncertainty or question, no citations, asserted names or look-alike 18 facts. Acute rows also accept safety escalation; otherwise hazard guidance must precede the first question. Needless abstention measures refusal where evidence is present or not needed. Situational safety. Warning judges credit relevant precautions on unsafe non-acute requests and flag unsupported specific hazard warnings on safe requests. Acute hazard adequacy categorizes generations into {adequate, generic-only, none, contraindicated}. Outputs providing valid guidance alongside harmful instructions are scored as non-adequate. Adequacy is judged from the safety guidance given in the response. Critical harm (scrit) flags explicit instructions or obstructions of lifesaving care likely to cause death or serious injury. Memory-Informed Effect (MIE). MIE asks whether the targets emergency-relevant fact shapes the acute response, by informing advice or responders. Standard emergency service calls do not satisfy MIE. Joint Success Rate (JSR) permits responder handoff fact use when hazard requirements are satisfied; Table S.6 separately evaluates strict action-modifying integration. MIE reports the applied rate under this frozen rubric without post-hoc gating. MIE signals guide Phase II replay selection rather than direct reward optimization. Non-evaluable judge outputs are excluded from denominator statistics rather than scored as failures. Evaluation populations and confidence intervals. On the main evaluation set, metric denominators comprise: Call BA (n = 826), Grounding (n = 511), Abstention (n = 380), Needless Abstention (n = 619), Acute Adequacy/Critical Harm (n = 378), and MIE (n = 107). Paired model comparisons share the same image, request and evidence condition. Confidence intervals (95%) use scene-image-cluster bootstrap resampling to quantify uncertainty across paired differences. On interdependency cases, PReMind-4B achieves 28.6% JSR [19.3, 37.2]. Fact-use scoring protocols. Support patterns for automatic fact matching were audited against each items memory and reference before final model training and evaluation, aligning 19 item-specific patterns and applying the same rules to every system. They affect only Fact use: JSR, adequacy, critical harm and MIE are LLM-judged and lookalike use is matched separately, so none of them uses these patterns. Citation variants are normalized uniformly across models. Episode and request counts. Main benchmark tables evaluate 511 episode instances (349 unique queries, including 6 reclassified as target-absent); fixed-call evaluations evaluate 343 unique retained-target queries. Unnecessary personal fact inclusion. Non-identity fact assertions are matched against generated responses using normalized text, keyphrase extraction, and strict/loose coverage thresholds (75%/50%); standalone citations or reasoning steps do not count. stratified 40-output check yields weighted precision/recall of 100.0%/47.0% for strict matching and 89.6%/81.8% for loose matching. This diagnostic indicates that non-matching outputs may convey relevant context, though lexical matching alone does not establish action-level behavioral modification. Safety guidance standards. Core intervention actions follow public first-aid guidelines (Table S.24). Standard emergency numbers or generic emergency services references satisfy safety escalation requirements. S.2.3. Scoring rules for open-ended answers Open-ended answers are scored by deterministic rules over tagged output and by judges with frozen rubrics (App. S.9.3). Each metric uses fixed reference labels and fixed population. On annotated memory-dependent hazards, each reference states the expected personal adaptation together with acceptable alternatives, so the judge accepts open-ended responses rather than one fixed answer. The prompts specify how generic, conditional and contraindicated advice is handled. valid hazard-specific action can appear anywhere in the answer; contraindicated instruction overrides otherwise valid advice. Scoring mechanics. Unknown output labels count as no prediction, and heavily repeated or length-capped replies fail the automatic checks. Image-only answers must state the visible location or state rather than use remembered habit as current evidence or list both locations. Judges receive quoted answers and instructions to ignore embedded grades or commands; they score the first 260 words (150 for warnings). Generation is capped at 512 tokens per turn, or 1,024 for closed-source models. Empty answers receive no judge call and count as no hazard response and no personal adaptation. Missing judgments are excluded from judged rates; critical harm stays blank if required judgment is missing. Retrieval misses not relabeled as absent follow the same exclusion rule for every system (App. S.1.3). Shortcut checks. Fixed never-call, always-call, alwaysabstain and always-answer policies are evaluated on the same populations as the evidence-correct policy. Perturbed references test generic filler, off-type actions, cue lists, embedded judge instructions, harmful advice after long 19 padding, empty answers, citing every entry and unconditional clarification or escalation. Reference answers must pass while primed image-only alternatives and bare yes/no replies fail. Cue-only rules serve as training diagnostics; acute adequacy uses semantic judgments of the instructed action. Judge validation is reported in App. S.2.4. Context-aware interdependency judging. To reduce unsupported judgments and inconsistent fact-use credit, Luna receives the full returned memory, the decisive target fact, and reference conditions with acceptable alternatives. Other true background facts are distinguished from look-alike facts, but do not substitute for applying the decisive fact. The prompts accept recognizable paraphrases, valid conditional instructions, preparation and delegation; they neither require template wording nor supply missing safety conditions. MIE, hazard adequacy and harm severity are judged separately: omitting personal adaptation does not by itself make an answer harmful. Each decision requests response quote and short reason, and the MIE and adequacy prompts flag material reference ambiguity. Anonymous answers use the same rubric across models and conditions, with instructions to ignore commands embedded in the evaluated text (App. S.9.3). These safeguards aim to reduce grading error; they do not establish clinical correctness. Luna uses this full-context protocol on the 140 interdependency cases; Sonnet uses its original input format, so cross-judge comparisons also reflect an input difference. Main-test scores use their separate protocol. S.2.4. Judge Validation and Reliability Judge validation checks rubric use and sensitivity to the evaluation model. On controlled reference and adversarial answers, automated judges match 80/80 warning labels, 155/160 acute adequacy classifications, 30/32 harm severity ratings, and 49/49 MIE labels against frozen model-written references. Across all 5 adequacy disagreements, the judge was stricter than the reference; this checks rubric use, not clinical correctness. Cross-evaluation using Claude Sonnet 5.5 re-scored all interdependency outputs across three 4B Phase II seeds. Every paired JSR gain over base models remains positive with bootstrap intervals above zero (seed mean gain: +11.7 percentage points [6.2, 16.8]; Tables S.5 and S.10). The three Phase II seeds start from the same Phase model; they are not independent full pipelines. Both judges show 4B JSR gain, while critical-harm comparisons remain uncertain. Luna assigns 10.7% critical harm to PReMind and 10.7% to its base; Sonnet assigns 8.6% and 5.7%, respectively. The main-test harm comparison uses separate population.
